1.pericope_label: Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob... This he ordained in Joseph for a testimony, when he went out through the land of Egypt

schools.summary: Delitzsch describes the psalm's construction, combining the lyric quality of one earlier Asaphic psalm with the didactic quality of another, and accounts for its abrupt close by the author's habit of ascending to his subject's height and descending into its depth without returning to where he began; on the Egyptian burdens he fills in the basket for carrying clay and bricks and cites a papyrus naming the people who dragged stones for the great watchtower of the city of Rameses. Ellicott corrects the opening phrase to strike up a tune, notes of the horn that it is the only ancient Hebrew instrument still in use on solemn occasions, and is cautious about the date: standing alone the phrase might mean the beginning of any month, and while a long array of authorities renders the second phrase the time appointed, in the only other place the word occurs the Latin gives after many days, the margin new moon, and two ancient translators full moon — which he thinks better supported. At the last verse he argues that the verb of going out cannot have Israel for subject on any sense of the preposition, so God must be the subject, moving over or against the land of Egypt.

Gill reads the new moon of the seventh month, the day of trumpets, and takes the statute to be of divine institution rather than a device of the children of Israel. Calvin divides the psalm in two, an exhortation to remember the grace that delivered the people and then God upbraiding them for refusing the yoke of the law, and notes that opinions vary widely as to the occasion.

Clarke thinks it generally agreed that the psalm was written for or used at the Feast of Trumpets, held on the first of Tisri at the opening of the Jewish year and still used in Jewish worship on that day, and adds the tradition, credited by many learned Christians, that the world was created in that month. He catalogues the instruments — the drum, the harp he takes for a sistrum, the psaltery which the Greek rendered a cithara, and the horn — and turns the verse into an argument against instrumental music in church. At the last verse he states the difficulty plainly, who heard and what was heard, and reports that every version but the Chaldee reads the pronoun in the third person. Wesley keeps the received first person and explains it of the progenitors, since all the generations of Israel make one body and are sometimes spoken of as one person, taking the unknown language for Egyptian.

Spurgeon presses manner and reason both in the summons to sing: in tune and measure so that public praise may be in harmony, and aloud, since no dulness should stupify our psalmody nor half-heartedness make it limp, God's acts of love speaking more loudly than any words of gratitude can. Henry adds that we do not come to church to sleep or be idle, our errand being to give God the glory due to his name.

Augustine takes the word rendered presses in the title for a mystery rather than farm equipment and reads it of the Church: in a press there is pressure, and of the pressure two results, one laid up and one thrown away, so that the treading and the crushing and the weight all belong to the figure.

debates.question: Which festival day is meant, and what does the second phrase mean?

positions.view: The Feast of Trumpets on the first of Tisri, at the opening of the Jewish year — and the psalm is still used in Jewish worship on that day.
The new moon of the seventh month, the day of blowing of trumpets.

Undecided: the first phrase might mean the beginning of any month, and the second is rendered the time appointed by many authorities but full moon by two ancient translators, which is better supported.
The significance matters more than the date: the feast is a divine institution deriving from the redemption under Moses.
Not fixed; the occasion is variously judged, and what matters is the psalm's two-part shape.

debates.question: Who heard the unfamiliar language, and what was it?

positions.view: The text should probably read in the third person, as every version but the Chaldee does; the language is either the Egyptian or the declaration God made by Moses.
The first person stands, and means the progenitors, since all the generations of Israel make one body; the language is Egyptian, unfamiliar because they lived apart.
The question of the hearer is secondary to the subject of the verb, which cannot be Israel and must be God, moving over or against the land of Egypt.
The verse is read of God's good will to Israel and their duty of obedience, without pressing the pronoun.

outliers.note: Turns the catalogue of instruments into a polemic: in a representative religion such as the Jewish there was necessarily much outside work, emblematic of better things, but a man must be ill off for proofs in favour of instrumental music in church who has recourse to the Jewish ritual.
Reads the word for presses in the psalm's title as an allegory of the Church under pressure, in which the treading separates what is to be laid up from what is to be thrown away.

themes: Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob.
Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery.
Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day.
For this was a statute for Israel, and a law of the God of Jacob.
This he ordained in Joseph for a testimony, when he went out through the land of Egypt: where I heard a language that I understood not.

6.pericope_label: I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots... I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it

schools.summary: Ellicott derives the second noun of the sixth verse from a root meaning to boil and so refers it to the potteries which with the brick-kilns made up the scene of the forced labour, setting aside the Greek and Latin reading that puts a basket here since the basket on the Egyptian monuments is what the previous clause means. At the seventh verse he declines the received verb altogether, holding that a scholar is right to derive it from a root meaning to cover rather than to answer, so that the line says God sheltered his people in the thundercloud, with plain allusion to the pillar of cloud; and he reads the recital as liturgical, the rehearsal of God's past dealings customary at the autumn feast, delivered as though the feast were in progress. On the promise of the tenth verse he supplies a Persian royal custom and an eastern table manner. Delitzsch describes the turn the discourse takes here, from festival to sorrow and awe, Israel's disobedience having frustrated the gracious purpose of its God's commandments and promises, and notes that the two names, my people and Israel, alternate as in the prophet's complaint.

Gill has the heavy loads of bricks carried on the shoulder, and defines the strange god by what engrosses a man rather than what stands in a shrine: whatever a man loves most or trusts in is his god, so friend or relation, wife or children may be set up in God's place, while the epicure makes a god of his belly, the covetous man of his money, and the self-righteous man of his own righteousness.

Clarke places the answering at Sinai, where God was heard but not seen, and keeps the closing promise abstract: let a man's desires be as extensive as they will, God undertakes to gratify them on condition of faithfulness, so that he shall lack no manner of thing that is good. Wesley places the same answering at the sea, the thunder coming from the dark and cloudy pillar against the Egyptians.

Henry turns the call to hear into a question — who should hear God if his own people will not, since he has already heard and answered them — and observes that the demand is not merely for a hearing but for being ruled; and yet, reasonable as it is, God puts an if upon it, because their neck is an iron sinew. He keeps to the ground of the promise rather than its figure, reminding the people what they owe to one who speaks as the Lord their God and redeemer from Egypt. Spurgeon asks whether the people can be so insensible as to be deaf to God himself, notes that he has to ask earnestly for a hearing, and turns it on the reader, since we are not fond of being upbraided and fly even from gentle reproofs.

debates.question: Where, and what, was the answer in the secret place of thunder?

positions.view: At Sinai, where God was heard but not seen.
At the sea, the thunder coming from the dark and cloudy pillar against the Egyptians.
Not an answering at all: the verb comes from a root meaning to cover, so God sheltered his people in the thundercloud, in allusion to the pillar of cloud.
The deliverance is the point rather than the place: they cried in their distress and he heard and brought them out of all their troubles.
Not addressed; the verse marks where the festival discourse turns to sorrow and awe.

debates.question: What does the promise to fill an opened mouth picture?

positions.view: Desire without limit, gratified on the sole condition of faithfulness, so that a man lacks no manner of thing that is good.

A court custom: a Persian king honouring a visitor would have him open his mouth wide and then cram it with sweetmeats and sometimes jewels, as it is still a mark of eastern politeness to put the daintiest morsel into a guest's mouth.
Not the figure but its ground: what the people owe to one who speaks as the Lord their God and their redeemer from Egypt.

outliers.note: Illustrates the opened mouth from Persian court practice, where the king would cram an honoured visitor's mouth with sweetmeats and sometimes with jewels.

Says of a man who will not hearken to God that the deaf adder is no more grovelling, and that where false gods are their worship follows, since while the nests remain the birds will be eager to return.

themes: I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots.
Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah.
Hear, O my people, and I will testify unto thee: O Israel, if thou wilt hearken unto me;
There shall no strange god be in thee; neither shalt thou worship any strange god.
I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.

11.pericope_label: But my people would not hearken to my voice; and Israel would none of me... He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the noun of the twelfth verse, taking it not for lust but for stubbornness or perversity, from a root meaning to twist; refers the submission of the fifteenth verse to Israel rather than to God, since the Lord's enemies are Israel's too, and explains the shift of number in the next clause as one of the sudden changes frequent in Hebrew poetry; and sets out the grammatical difficulty of the last verse, where the proper rendering gives he fed them and satisfied thee, but the change of person is harsh and the past tense sits badly where nothing in fact happened, so that he would slightly alter the pointing to give would feed. Delitzsch prints these closing verses without any comment, the block breaking off at the quotation.

Gill gives the refusal a figure from elsewhere in the Psalter, the deaf adder stopping its ear against the charmer's voice; ranks the giving over to a man's own heart's lust above ordinary chastisement and even above being delivered to Satan, since salvation may follow the one and damnation the other, while holding it a righteous judgment nonetheless; distinguishes God's purposing will from his commanding and approving will at the wish of the thirteenth verse; notes that the verb of the fourteenth means to bring enemies to their knees; and prefers the harder rendering at the fifteenth, that the haters should have lied unto him in a feigned submission, instancing the emperor said to have cried when wounded that the Galilean had overcome him.

Clarke describes the mechanism of the judgment, that God withdrew the restraining grace they had abused and left them to their own inventions; praises the Hebrew of the thirteenth verse as the most plaintive thing he knows, in which sense and sound are surprisingly united, saying that he has never found in any poet, Greek or Latin, a finer example of deep-seated grief unable to express itself without interruptions of sighs and sobs; draws the consequence that where the promise appeared to fail it was because they rejected God's counsel, since while they were faithful not one jot of his word failed them; and closes by quoting an old English psalter's version of the last verse with its christological paraphrase. Wesley takes the honey of the last verse for all pleasant and precious fruits.

debates.question: What does the wish of the thirteenth verse express?

positions.view: Not God's purposing will, since none has resisted that and he could have given them ears to hear, but his commanding and approving will, that men should hearken to the declarations he has made.
The question is not raised: the line is the finest example of deep-seated grief in any poetry, sense and sound surprisingly united, and is to be heard rather than resolved.
Left without comment; the block prints the verse and breaks off.

debates.question: How should the last verse be read?

positions.view: The pointing should be slightly changed to give 'I would feed them', since the proper rendering's change of person is harsh and its past tense sits badly where nothing in fact happened.
As it stands, the Hebrew giving the fat of the wheat, with the honey standing for all pleasant and precious fruits.

As the older English tradition read it, of the wheat as the body of Christ and spiritual understanding and the honey from the stone as a wisdom sweet to the heart — several of the fathers understanding the place of Christ.

outliers.note: Judges the Hebrew of the thirteenth verse against all classical poetry, saying he has never found in any poet, Greek or Latin, a finer example of grief unable to express itself without sighs and sobs, and transliterates the line so it may be heard.
Illustrates the submission of God's haters with the emperor who is said to have cried when wounded that the Galilean had overcome him.

themes: But my people would not hearken to my voice; and Israel would none of me.
So I gave them up unto their own hearts’ lust: and they walked in their own counsels.
Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways!
I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries.
The haters of the Lord should have submitted themselves unto him: but their time should have endured for ever.
He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee.
